6
A tennis ball is thrown horizontally in air from the top of a tall building.
The effect of air resistance is not negligible.
What happens to the horizontal and to the vertical components of the ball’s velocity?
vertical component
horizontal component
of velocity
of velocity
A
constant
constant
B
constant
increases at a constant rate
C
decreases to zero
increases at a constant rate
D
decreases to zero
increases to a maximum value

hints: Notice the ball is thrown horizontally, so initially all its speed is horizontal and vertical speed is zero, with air resistance opposing each component of motion.
Recall drag force increases with speed, so horizontal drag slows the horizontal motion with no force to sustain it, while vertical drag increasingly opposes weight.
Connect the vertical forces to terminal velocity: net downward force and downward acceleration shrink as the ball falls faster until drag equals weight.
walkthrough: Identify the motion: initial velocity is purely horizontal, initial vertical velocity is zero, with weight acting vertically down and air resistance opposing the instantaneous velocity.

Consider the horizontal direction: there is no horizontal driving force after release, only the horizontal component of air resistance acting backward, so $F_{net,x} < 0$ and the horizontal component of velocity must decrease.
As horizontal speed falls, horizontal drag $\propto$ speed also falls, so the deceleration lessens and horizontal velocity tends toward zero rather than reversing.
Consider the vertical direction: weight $mg$ down causes downward acceleration, but upward air resistance grows as downward vertical speed grows, so net downward force $mg - D_v$ decreases.
Therefore vertical acceleration decreases from $g$ toward zero, so vertical speed increases ever more slowly and approaches a maximum terminal value where $D_v = mg$.
This combination of horizontal velocity decreasing to zero and vertical velocity increasing to a maximum value is option D.

A.explanation: Neither component stays constant because air resistance opposes motion and weight accelerates the ball downward.

B.explanation: Without air resistance horizontal velocity would be constant and vertical velocity would increase at constant rate $g$, but air resistance is stated to be not negligible.

C.explanation: Horizontal drag does reduce horizontal velocity toward zero, but vertical acceleration cannot stay at $g$ because upward air resistance grows as vertical speed grows.

D.explanation: Horizontal drag with no forward force reduces horizontal velocity toward zero, while vertical speed approaches terminal velocity where drag balances weight.
